claims.text: The initial NbMoTaW alloy is single-phase.
NbMoTaW has comparatively high high-temperature strength.
Controlled additions of both Ti and V to NbMoTaW will improve its strength–plasticity combination.
Conventional melting and homogenization can produce a single-phase Ti/V-modified NbMoTaW alloy.
Ti addition increases grain-boundary cohesion in NbMoTaW.
V addition enhances lattice distortion and solute strengthening in NbMoTaW.
The Ti and V additions help maintain a stable microstructure.
Ti improves ductility by strengthening grain boundaries.
V activates precipitation or hardening mechanisms that increase yield strength.
The effects of Ti and V are synergistic, producing a balance of strength and plasticity.
The Ti/V-modified alloy will attain room-temperature ductility approaching or exceeding 11.5%.
The Ti/V-modified alloy will maintain or increase high-temperature yield strength relative to NbMoTaW.
V alloying has been reported to increase yield strength from 1058 MPa to about 1246 MPa.
Yield-strength values around 1246 MPa are applicable to testing near 1150 °C.
The benefit requires Ti and V contents within an optimal range while retaining a single-phase refractory alloy.
Excessive Ti or V additions can promote brittle secondary phases or phase separation and negate the benefits.
Identically processed baseline and modified samples tested for room-temperature plastic strain, high-temperature yield strength, and phase constitution can evaluate the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The alloy is required to remain single-phase, but V is also said to operate through precipitation hardening, which ordinarily implies formation of a distinct precipitate phase. The hypothesis does not explain how these statements are compatible.
The predicted outcome describes total ductility approaching or exceeding 11.5%, whereas the falsification rule refers to an approximately 11.5% improvement, which is a different metric.

Secondary-phase formation is declared outside the conditions under which improvement is expected, yet the experiment treats formation of secondary brittle phases as falsification rather than as failure to satisfy the stated boundary conditions.
